The route of the Byway now fully encircles the lake and connects the downtown areas of Newbury, New London and Sunapee.

evidence.claim: From New London, travel west on Route 11 through Georges Mills, then south toward Sunapee Harbor.
evidence.quote: New Hampshire Route 11 runs through the village, leading east to New London and south to the center of Sunapee.

evidence.quote: Before Sunapee was a sizable tourist attraction, it was an industrial area. One factory produced 110 clothespins a minute.

evidence.claim: Hames Park, beside the Sugar River on an old factory site, interprets that manufacturing history.
evidence.quote: In Sunapee Harbor, Hames Park along the Sugar River is located on the site of an old factory and interprets the manufacturing history of the town.

evidence.quote: The Sunapee Historical Society Museum is located in the historic Osborne-Flanders Stable

evidence.quote: The pilothouse of the Kearsarge was salvaged from the lake in the 1960s and is on display at the Sunapee Historical Center.

evidence.quote: Lake Station connecting the rail line to steamboats that circled the lake, stopping at the various villages and grand hotels.

evidence.claim: An antique caboose now commemorates the railroad that brought vacationers here.
evidence.quote: Today, the village contains a colorful antique caboose commemorating the railroad line that passed by, bringing vacationers from other parts of the country.

evidence.claim: The railroad museum and Center Meeting House interpret that period and its effects on the region.
evidence.quote: Today, the railroad museum and the Center Meeting House provide insight into the history of that era and its impact on the region.

evidence.quote: The Center Meetinghouse occupies a prominent site in the center of Newbury's main village, overlooking the southern end of Lake Sunapee at the eastern corner of the junction of New Hampshire Routes 103 and 103A.

evidence.claim: Inside the meetinghouse, original box pews face a carved pulpit at the rear of the main chamber.
evidence.quote: It has its original box pews, oriented to face the rear of the main chamber, where the decoratively carved pulpit is in an elevated position between the two entrance aisles.

evidence.claim: The main entrance of The Fells’ first cottage faced the lake because the Hay family arrived by boat.
evidence.quote: The main entrance of the primary cottage faced the lake, as the Hay family arrived by boat.

evidence.claim: The estate was John Hay’s summer home; he served as secretary of state from 1898 until his death in 1905.
evidence.quote: He became United States Secretary of State in 1898, serving in that position until his death in 1905.

evidence.claim: The estate was John Hay’s summer home
evidence.quote: The Fells, also known as the Hay Estate, was originally the summer home of John Milton Hay

evidence.claim: Architect George Hammond directed its construction in 1891; a guest cottage followed beside it in 1897.
evidence.quote: The first cottage on the property was constructed in 1891 under the direction of architect George Hammond. In 1897, a second guest cottage was added beside the original.

evidence.claim: After John Hay’s death, his son Clarence and Clarence’s wife Alice transformed the summer cottages.
evidence.quote: Clarence and his wife Alice (née: Appleton) began to transform the rustic summer cottages into more of a lakeside mansion.

evidence.claim: After John Hay’s death, his son Clarence
evidence.quote: After Hay's death in 1905, the property was handed down to his son, Clarence Hay.

evidence.claim: Renovations beginning in 1915 gave the house a Colonial Revival design and turned the connecting breezeway into a formal hall, joining the cottages as one house.
evidence.quote: Starting in 1915, under the supervision of local architect Prentice Sanger, Clarence and Alice had the house renovated into the Colonial Revival style. The breezeway connecting the two cottages was transformed into a formal hallway, so that the two cottages became part of one house.

evidence.claim: A garage was added later as automobile use grew.
evidence.quote: A garage was later added to accommodate the growing use of automobiles.
